justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are driven by the trends and patterns I observe in the underlying data. For the 1-day outlook, the point estimate is heavily influenced by the most recent information, as shorter time horizons rely predominantly on immediate momentum, small fluctuations, or short-term dependencies in the system being analyzed. Over the course of a week, the 1-week estimate adjusts slightly but still reflects current trends, while factoring in the likelihood of small natural variations in the system. By the 1-month horizon, the forecast considers the possibility of broader trends or emerging cycles, resulting in a modest upward adjustment to 71.7.

Uncertainty widens as the time horizon grows because predicting further into the future introduces greater unknowns. For the 1-day forecast, the confidence interval is relatively narrow because the system is unlikely to experience major shifts in such a short time frame—recent trends tend to dominate over random noise. By the 1-week mark, there is more time for small perturbations or external influences to accumulate and introduce variability. At the 1-month horizon, the uncertainty has grown further because there is more room for unexpected disruptions, longer-term shifts, or the effects of external factors that are harder to predict accurately. Thus, the widening of the confidence intervals reflects this increasing range of plausible outcomes.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated intervals if there were sudden, extreme events or major structural changes in the system being analyzed. For example, if the forecast relates to financial markets, unexpected news such as a global economic shock or major policy announcement could disrupt trends and produce outcomes well beyond what was anticipated. If the forecast pertains to the weather or climate, severe storms or rare patterns could also produce results outside the bounds of the confidence intervals. These types of outlier events are difficult to predict, and while they are captured probabilistically to some extent in the construction of the forecasts, extreme deviations are always a possibility in any model.
